(1) "A person," etc. In order to make the distinctions in this siman easier to understand, I will first give a brief introduction based on the Gemara and the halachic decisors. Two verses are written. One states, "so that your servant and your maidservant may rest like you." This refers to a slave who underwent brit milah and immersion for the sake of slavery and accepted all the mitzvot incumbent upon a slave, meaning all the mitzvot in which a woman is obligated. Shabbos is therefore included, and he may not perform melacha on Shabbos. This verse teaches that the obligation of the slave's rest also rests upon his master, who is commanded to prevent him from performing melacha even for the slave's own needs. Another verse states, "and the son of your maidservant and the stranger shall be refreshed." The Sages expounded this as referring to a slave bodily owned by a Jew who did not undergo brit milah and immersion but accepted the 7 Noahide mitzvot. His master must prevent him from performing melacha for the master on Shabbos, and likewise every Jew is forbidden by Torah law to instruct him to perform melacha for them on Shabbos. For his own needs, however, such a slave may perform melacha on Shabbos, because Shabbos is not among the 7 Noahide mitzvot. His law is like that of a ger toshav, who is not commanded concerning Shabbos, although a Jew is still forbidden by Torah law to instruct him to perform melacha for the Jew, as indicated by the verse. Regarding a slave bodily owned by a Jew who did not undergo brit milah or immersion and did not accept even the 7 Noahide mitzvot, the authorities disagree whether we are likewise commanded concerning his rest, as will be explained.

(2) "Concerning the rest of his slave." The master is commanded to guard him and prevent him from performing melacha even for the slave's own needs, as stated above. It is permitted to lease such a slave to a non-Jew during the weekdays if he stipulates that the non-Jew not have him perform melacha on Shabbos. This differs from one's animal, concerning which siman 246, seif 3, states that one may not lease it to a non-Jew under such an arrangement because the non-Jew is not trusted to honor the condition. Here, the non-Jew cannot force the slave to work against his will, and the slave is trusted concerning this. [Pri Megadim]

(3) "Those that apply to a slave." Meaning all mitzvot in which a woman is obligated.

(4) "He is like a ger toshav." A ger toshav is one who accepted the 7 Noahide mitzvot and undertook not to serve idolatry, even in partnership.

(5) "For himself." Meaning his own melacha, such as sewing his garments, repairing his shoes, and the like, or working for wages in order to have food beyond what his master supplies him.

(6) "But not for his master." Even if the master did not explicitly instruct him to perform the melacha, it is forbidden, because ordinarily he acts with his master's interest in mind, and the Torah warned the master to prevent this, as stated above in seif katan 1. Even rabbinic melacha is forbidden for the master's benefit. Some are lenient regarding rabbinic melacha if the master did not explicitly instruct him.

(7) "And it is forbidden to every Jew." Meaning by Torah law. Since he has already accepted the 7 Noahide mitzvot, everyone agrees that he has the status of a ger toshav, and the Torah forbids a Jew to have melacha performed through him.

(8) "And if he did not accept." Meaning that even if he accepted no mitzvah at all, nevertheless, since he is a slave bodily owned by a Jew, this view holds that his law is the same as one who accepted the 7 Noahide mitzvot, and it is forbidden for him to perform melacha for any Jew.

(9) "To tell a Jewish-owned slave." Only telling an ordinary non-Jew, which is a rabbinic shevut, was permitted in the cases mentioned there. A non-Jewish slave owned by a Jew, concerning whom the Torah commands rest, has no such permission except for pikuach nefesh.

(10) "And some disagree and permit this." This refers to a slave who is a complete non-Jew and accepted no mitzvot. Although the first view equates him with one who accepted the 7 Noahide mitzvot and therefore forbids even another Jew to instruct him, the dissenting view holds that the Torah prohibited only melacha performed for his master, as indicated by "the son of your maidservant shall be refreshed." For another Jew he is no more stringent than an ordinary non-Jew, so the prohibition is only rabbinic and it is therefore permitted for the needs of an ill person even where there is no danger.

(11) "If he was doing," etc. Although it was explained above that the master is commanded concerning the slave's rest, whether the slave accepted the 7 mitzvot or not, that applies specifically when the master is pleased with this melacha, for then we assume that the slave ordinarily acts with the master's interests in mind and the master must stop him. If it is evident that the slave is not acting for the master, it is treated like melacha for himself and the master need not prevent it.

(12) "And for another Jew," etc. Specifically regarding his master, because he is his slave, we assume that whatever he does is for his master. Regarding another Jew, even if the slave acts knowing that the Jew will benefit, as long as the Jew did not instruct him and the slave or ger toshav began on his own, we assume that he principally acts for his own benefit in order to profit from the work. It is forbidden only when the Jew instructs him, as stated above in seif katan 7.

(13) "It is permitted." See the end of siman 252, seif 2, where in some circumstances one must nevertheless protest on rabbinic grounds.

(14) "Provided that he does not benefit." This is rabbinic, because the slave is no better than an ordinary non-Jew who performs melacha knowingly for a Jew, from whose melacha the Jew may not benefit on Shabbos, as stated at the beginning of siman 276.

(15) "And some say that every," etc. They hold that the Torah warned concerning a Jewish-owned slave on Shabbos only where he has at least some mitzvot upon him, meaning the 7 Noahide mitzvot, as explained in Beit Yosef. See Eliyah Rabbah, who cites several authorities that in practice one should be stringent like the first view. It is forbidden to instruct an apostate Jew or Karaites to perform melacha for him on Shabbos or Yom Tov, because of lifnei iver. [Pri Megadim]

(16) "And every slave," etc. Whether this also refers to a slave who did not undergo brit milah and immersion, see Tosefet Shabbos and Pri Megadim.

(17) "It is forbidden to go out," etc. The ruling is first stated generally and then explained. If there are 2 grounds for leniency, namely the seal is made of clay and hangs from his neck, he may go out wearing it. There is no concern that he will remove it and carry it 4 amot in a public domain, because he fears his master will say that he removed it to appear free. There is likewise no concern that it will break by itself in the public domain and that he will carry the broken piece home, because a broken clay seal has no value. Holding it in his hand would not prove his servitude, because it signifies servitude only when it is hanging from his neck or garment. If there is only 1 ground for leniency, however, either because the seal is hanging from his garment or because the seal is metal and valuable, he may not go out with it into a public domain, as explained below.

(18) "But not on his garment." Perhaps the seal will break by itself and he will fear his master will say that he removed it in order to appear free. He may then fold his garment so the place of the seal is not visible and carry the garment upon his shoulder, which makes the garment a burden.

(19) "And with a metal one," etc. Since it is valuable and his master is particular that it not be lost, we are concerned that it may break and he will carry it 4 amot in a public domain.

(20) "In every manner." Meaning even when it hangs from his neck. Since he made the seal for himself, he does not fear his master if he removes it, and we therefore fear that he will take it in his hand and carry it 4 amot in a public domain.

"And with a metal one." See Ateret Zekenim. Regarding a slave who did not undergo brit milah and immersion, according to the first view, which holds that there is a Torah prohibition against his performing melacha for his master, one may say that he may not go out with a metal seal. If the seal breaks, he will bring it to his master, acting for his master's benefit, and this is forbidden, as Levush states explicitly. With a clay seal attached to his garment, however, where he folds the garment because he fears his master and his master derives no benefit from that, it is permitted for such a slave. Accordingly the law is reversed with a metal seal: where his master made it, it is forbidden whether it hangs from his garment or neck, because the master is particular about the broken pieces and the slave will bring it to the master for the master's benefit. If the slave made it for himself, it is permitted in every manner, because he is allowed to perform melacha for himself. A slave who underwent brit milah and immersion, however, is forbidden in every case when he made it for himself, whether the seal is clay or metal, as we explained. With God's help I will explain more elsewhere.

However, even if before Shabbos he stated that he does not wish to keep it as a brit milah knife but only as an ordinary knife, one can say that this does not help. In siman 310, seif 7, in Rama's gloss regarding a money purse, designation is not removed unless he performs an act, such as opening it at the bottom and thereby removing it from its special designation. There the purse is muktzeh machmat chisaron kis, and it appears that one cannot cancel its designation before Shabbos merely by speech, but only through an act. As for what Magen Avraham writes in siman 308, seif katan 40, regarding palm branches, that since they stand for firewood just as they can stand for sitting, the thought of using them for sitting can remove the thought that had designated them for burning: one must say that a money purse is different. Since he designated it for money and actually placed money into it, there was an act, and a mere thought cannot undo that act. Palm branches are different because scraping or preparing them is not considered an act proving designation for burning, since that preparation may also be needed for sitting. Accordingly, regarding a brit milah knife that was actually used for brit milah, and likewise a slaughtering knife that was actually used for slaughter, one can say that verbal declaration alone does not cancel the special designation unless there is an act. All this requires further study for practical halacha.

"For the wealthy." Taz writes that the general rule is as follows: something fit for poor people, when it is in the house of a poor person, is muktzeh for wealthy people because it is not fit for them. Nevertheless, a wealthy person who is present in the poor person's house follows the status of that house. But something that is muktzeh for a wealthy person and is in the wealthy person's house is forbidden even to all poor people, as though the wealthy person had already thrown it into the refuse. See there.

"Returned." Taz writes that the same applies to a scalpel used for a brit milah on Shabbos. At bein hashmashot it was muktzeh machmat chisaron kis, like a scribe's knife, because a person is very particular not to use that scalpel for any other purpose lest it become damaged, and certainly he does not use it for eating, which is contrary to ordinary human behavior. Therefore, although it is designated for the mitzvah of brit milah on the following day, once its needed use has ended it returns to the prohibition of moving that applied at bein hashmashot. It should therefore be put away in the same room in which the brit milah was performed. Maharil writes likewise; see Yoreh De'ah, siman 266. Bach, siman 308, permits moving it, and Maharshal writes likewise. Magen Avraham, siman 331, seif katan 5, discusses this at length and concludes that one should be stringent not to put it down until he has brought it home, because any muktzeh object already in one's hand may be carried to any place one wishes. See there, and see Beit Yaakov, siman 102.

(14) "Whether regarding a prohibition of eating," etc. The phrase "whether ... whether" teaches a greater novelty in the first case, regarding eating. It means that not only with respect to ordinary moving do we certainly say that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbos and therefore permit moving it once its muktzeh status has departed, but it is even permitted to eat it.

(15) "If something happened to it," etc. For example, rain fell on raisins and they swelled until they were unfit to eat, and afterward the sun shone upon them and they dried until they again became fit to eat. They return to their permitted status. The reason is that the concept of muktzeh for half of Shabbos does not apply when the item was fit at bein hashmashot. Taz writes that a scalpel used for a brit milah on Shabbos may not be moved after the brit milah, because it is muktzeh machmat chisaron kis: a person is particular not to use it for any other purpose. This is unlike those who permit moving it on the ground that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbos, because at bein hashmashot it too was muktzeh machmat chisaron kis and could not then be moved for any purpose. Therefore, even though it was designated for the mitzvah of brit milah the following day, once its needed use has ended it returns to the prohibition of moving that applied at bein hashmashot. It should therefore be put away in the same room in which the brit milah was performed. Magen Avraham in siman 331, seif katan 5, agrees with the basic law, but holds that one should be stringent in another respect: while the scalpel is still in his hand, he should not put it down until he places it in a guarded location or carries it home, because any muktzeh object already in one's hand may be moved to whatever place one wishes, as stated above in siman 308, seif 3. If the mohel also performs priyah and therefore must put down the scalpel, Eliyah Rabbah writes that another person should receive it directly from his hand and carry it to a guarded place. Nevertheless, after the fact, if he put it down and there is concern that it may be stolen, Eliyah Rabbah inclines to rely upon Rama and Shach, who hold that it may be moved. Chayei Adam cites this in the laws of brit milah.

(16) "It is forbidden for the entire day." The principal designation must be made before the day begins, as it is written, "And it shall be on the sixth day that they shall prepare that which they bring." This item, however, was set aside from use at the very beginning of the day.

"Returned to its permitted status." The reason is that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbos, since at bein hashmashot it was fit. In Yoreh De'ah, siman 266, I wrote that a scalpel used for a brit milah on Shabbos may not be moved after the brit milah, unlike Responsa Maharshal, which permits it on the ground that there is no muktzeh for half of Shabbos. That principle does not apply here, because at bein hashmashot the scalpel was not fit to be moved. It was muktzeh, like a scribe's knife in siman 308. I brought proof from the pestle upon which meat was cut, in the first chapter of Beitzah, 11a, and from the spit upon which meat was roasted on Yom Tov, in chapter Ein Tzedin. These 2 objects possess an inherent muktzeh status: the pestle because one is particular about it and assigns it a fixed place, like the implements discussed at the beginning of Perek Kol HaKelim, and the spit because it is merely a piece of wood taken for use as a spit and has no status of a utensil, as Tur writes in siman 518. They are therefore even more restrictive than a kli shemelachto l'issur. Although at bein hashmashot they were designated for melacha needed on Yom Tov, after the Yom Tov use ended they returned to their prior muktzeh prohibition. The very same applies to this scalpel. At bein hashmashot it was muktzeh machmat chisaron kis, like a scribe's knife. It is obvious that a person is very particular not to use such a scalpel for another purpose lest it be damaged, and certainly he does not use it for eating. Therefore, although it is designated for the mitzvah of brit milah on the following day, once its needed use has ended it returns to the prohibition of moving that applied at bein hashmashot.

I later saw in Yam Shel Shlomo, Perek Ein Tzedin, siman 16, that Maharshal maintained his position. He writes that the case is not comparable to dried figs and raisins, which are entirely unfit during their interim state because they become spoiled. A brit milah scalpel, however, is physically fit to eat with or for another permitted use even at bein hashmashot; the owner merely designates it for brit milah and not for another use. Therefore, he argues, it is not muktzeh, because in any event he has prepared it for Shabbos itself. A spit used for roasting is different because it becomes repulsive, while the scalpel does not remain repulsive if it is wiped clean. Nor, he argues, should its preservation for its special use return it to muktzeh machmat chisaron kis, because even at bein hashmashot it was designated for that same use. End quote. What I wrote above refutes all of this. The scalpel is exactly like the pestle and spit mentioned above and may not be moved except as needed for the brit milah. Afterward it should be put away in the same room in which the brit milah was performed. Maharil writes likewise. See also my discussion in Yoreh De'ah, siman 266.

"From wood smoke." I have not seen any of the great authorities practice this. Likewise, in Yoreh De'ah it is written that ideally the ink should be made from a substance derived from a tree, which implies that they were not particular that it specifically be made from smoke. Rambam writes that it is a mitzvah to write with ink that can be erased. Responsa Maharil, siman 127, writes that many great authorities validated our ink, as may be found in Hagahot Maimoniyot. Nevertheless, since Rabbeinu Tam invalidates gall-based ink, Rashi invalidates adramint, and other authorities invalidated glotshteyn, it is proper to be stringent in order to satisfy all opinions and to write with shtoftint, which is made from thorns, or with herbal ink, as Hagahot Maimoniyot writes. See also the second chapter of Shabbos, which implies that they made ink from the smoke of oils.
